headline: Maine State Archives launches online portal for more than 100,000 public records
dek: The new Open Access platform brings digitized and born-digital state records into one searchable site, while the archives continue a much larger preservation effort.
body: Maine’s State Archives has launched a public online portal that puts more than 100,000 imaged government and historical records in one searchable place. Secretary of State Shenna Bellows announced the official launch of Open Access on Oct. 1, describing it as the public-facing part of a broader effort to preserve and provide long-term access to records held by the state. StateScoop independently reported the rollout as an expansion of online access to Maine records.

The platform is available at [digitalarchives.maine.gov](https://digitalarchives.maine.gov/). Visitors can search the collection, browse by category and use list, timeline, gallery or map views. The site groups materials into areas including the executive and legislative branches, courts, land and natural resources, social history, military records, elections, statehood and government administration. The [Maine State Archives’ digital-records page](https://www.maine.gov/sos/archives/digital-archives) says documents in the online collection are public records and free to download.

The launch is significant because it covers both digitized material and records that were created electronically in the first place. That distinction matters for a government archive: scanning older paper documents makes them easier to use, while preserving born-digital files helps prevent newer public records from becoming inaccessible as software and storage systems change. Maine officials describe Open Access as part of a strategic digital-preservation system for records that are archival or subject to long-term retention.

The historical range is unusually broad. The Secretary of State’s announcement points to collections stretching from a 1639 royal land grant to the 2024 papers of the Lewiston Tragedy Commission. Other examples include Revolutionary War land grants, records from Maine’s Civil War history and documents tied to the state’s development. Those materials can serve different audiences: genealogists tracing families, students working with primary sources, researchers studying public policy and residents seeking a record of how state institutions operated.

The new portal does not mean the entire archive is online. The Maine State Archives says it cares for approximately eight miles of official state records, and officials acknowledge that much remains to be digitized. The launch announcement says Open Access currently contains just over 100,000 imaged records and will grow as more collections are scanned. The archives’ broader digital-archives information page separately reported more than one million individual records in its online collection as of March 1, a larger figure that includes the state’s wider digital-access work rather than only the newly highlighted imaged records on Open Access.

That difference gives readers a useful way to understand the project’s scale: Open Access is a new front door, not a finished inventory. Its search tools can make records discoverable without a trip to Augusta, but the results will still depend on what has been processed, described and digitized. The [Archives’ research guidance](https://www.maine.gov/sos/archives/archives-services) says the facility is a closed-stacks, non-circulating archive and that researchers should make appointments so staff can retrieve materials; the online catalog’s coverage will change as new collections are added.

For Maine communities, the practical benefit is a shorter path between a question and the original record. A resident investigating a land transaction, a teacher building a lesson about statehood or a researcher checking an agency decision can begin with the same public platform. The next phase is continued digitization and preservation: expanding the searchable holdings while keeping the records authentic, usable and available for future generations.
author: NorthEast News Desk
